title: DFS in Reykjavik: Find Paths the Deep Way
description: Watch DFS explore street-map nodes deep into the graph before it backtracks. You’ll see how depth-first traversal turns real-world navigation into a graph search visualization.
ig_caption:
🌍🗺️ Reykjavík (Vesturbær) street graph, but make it DFS.

In this visualization, **DFS (Depth-First Search)** starts from the origin node and commits to a path as deep as possible—using a **stack** (explicit or call stack) to remember where to backtrack. 🧠🔁 That means DFS doesn’t “optimize” for the shortest route by default; instead, it explores connectivity by diving through neighbors until it hits a dead-end, then it rewinds to the last choice point.

📌 Graph theory angle: we model intersections/blocks as a graph (nodes + edges). Real street maps become a **search space** where DFS can be tested for reachability, traversal order, and how backtracking reconstructs the eventual route to the goal. Why it’s powerful: it’s fast for discovering paths in large graphs—especially when the goal is “find any route,” not necessarily the shortest.

fb_caption:
🚶‍♂️🗺️ Reykjavík’s streets visualized as a graph! This reel demonstrates **DFS (Depth-First Search)**: it explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. In graph search terms, that means the order of visiting intersections depends on neighbor structure—perfect for learning how traversal works on real street-map graphs.

DFS Pathfinding Visualization in Reykjavík (Vesturbær)! 🌍🧠

In this YouTube Shorts-style reel, we turn a real street map into a graph (nodes=intersections/blocks, edges=roads) and use **DFS (Depth-First Search)** to explore deep paths first, then backtrack at dead-ends. Perfect for learning fundamentals of graph traversal, graph search, stacks vs recursion, and how traversal order affects the route found.
